sentences.text: Sena had been through Istanbul Airport six times before.
She was eleven, and her mother lived in Frankfurt and her father lived in Singapore, and Sena spent half of every year with each.
The direct flight was fifteen hours and expensive, so her parents flew her with a stop.
Turkish Airlines was the cheapest with the best service for children flying alone.
The stop was in Istanbul.
Twelve hours, most times.
She had learned to hate the twelve hours.
Twelve hours was too long to just wait in an airport but too short to leave and see the city — she was too young to leave the terminal alone.
Her flight from Frankfurt had landed at eight-thirty in the evening.
Her connecting flight to Singapore left at nine in the morning.
That was twelve and a half hours in the terminal.
The airline's people had walked her from the arriving gate to the transit area and had shown her the small kids' lounge where children flying alone could wait.
But she was old enough now that she was allowed to be in the general terminal too if she wanted.
She always wanted.
The kids' lounge was too full of small crying children and cartoons.
She preferred to sit in the huge quiet windows of the international terminal and watch the planes come and go.
She found her usual seating area — a quiet gate near the far end of the international terminal that did not have many flights at night.
She sat down.
She put her small backpack beside her.
She took out her book.
She tried to read for a while.
She could not concentrate.
She looked at her phone.
It was nine-forty-five p.m.
She still had eleven and a quarter hours to go.
She put her head against the glass of the window.
She watched a plane taxi past.
This flight always tired her.
Not because it was long — it was long, but she had done it so many times that it was routine.
It tired her because every time she flew, she was leaving one parent and going to the other.
Right now she was leaving her mother, whom she had lived with for six months, and going to her father, whom she had not seen in six months.
She loved her father.
She would be happy to see him.
But she would miss her mother very much.
And she knew that in six months she would fly back and it would be the reverse.
She loved both parents.
But she never felt fully at home anywhere.
She was always half-there.
At about ten-thirty an older woman sat down in the row of chairs — not next to Sena, but one over, with an empty seat between them.
She was maybe seventy.
She wore a modest dark dress and a soft rose-colored headscarf.
She had a small canvas bag on her lap.
She was holding a small paper cup of tea.
She sat down carefully, like her back hurt a little.
She did not look at Sena.
She just sat and looked out the window.
Sena did not really notice her for a while.
Sena kept trying to read her book.
At about eleven the old woman turned to Sena and said something in Turkish.
Sena said, in English, "I am sorry.
I do not speak Turkish." The old woman smiled a small smile.
She switched to English.
Her English was clear but slow.
She said, "I said — you have been sitting there for a long time.
Are you alone." Sena said, "Yes.
I am flying alone.
My flight is in the morning."
"Where are you going," said the old woman.
"To Singapore.
My father lives there." "Where are you coming from." "Frankfurt.
My mother lives there." The old woman nodded.
She said, "How long is your wait here." "Twelve and a half hours.
My flight is at nine tomorrow morning." The old woman was silent for a moment.
Then she said, "That is a long time to sit by a window.
My name is Nazan.
If you would like company, I am also waiting.
My flight is at eight in the morning.
If you would prefer to be alone, I understand."
Sena said, "You can stay.
Please stay.
I am — I am tired of being alone.
My name is Sena." Nazan smiled.
She moved one seat closer so they were sitting next to each other.
She said, "Would you like some tea.
I bought too much." She handed Sena the small paper cup.
It was still warm.
It was Turkish tea — strong and dark, with sugar.
Sena drank a small sip.
It was good.
For the first hour they talked about small things.
Nazan lived in Istanbul.
She was returning home.
She had been in Frankfurt visiting her son, who lived there.
She had a small apartment in a district called Kadıköy on the Asian side of the city.
She had been a music teacher for forty-five years — piano, mostly, and some voice.
She had retired ten years ago.
She lived alone now — her husband had died six years ago — but she was fine, she had many friends, and she saw her son and his family twice a year.
This trip had been the second one this year.
Sena told Nazan about her life.
About Frankfurt.
About Singapore.
About flying twice a year.
About the twelve-hour layover, which she had always hated.
Nazan listened carefully.
She did not interrupt.
She nodded.

When Sena had finished — she had talked for maybe fifteen minutes, which was longer than she had talked to anyone in a long time — Nazan said, quietly, "That is a hard life for an eleven-year-old, Sena.
Living in two places.
Missing one parent while you are with the other.
I want you to know that I hear that.
It is a real hard thing."
